title: For parents: leading faith at home
for: I'm a parent who wants to lead well
subtitle: Eight sessions for parents themselves: leading when no one showed you how, faith at each age, a child's hard questions, a doubting teenager, discipline and grace, parenting alone, and handing it on.
intro: This track is for mothers, fathers, grandparents and anyone raising children who wants to lead faith at home and isn't sure how. It sits beside Start at the table tonight, which gives a family the habit of the table. This one is about the parent: your fears, your own faith, the questions your children ask, and the seasons when it all feels harder than anyone said.

There are eight sessions of about ten minutes. Each has a short teaching, one page on this site to open and use, and then one question, one thing to do at home and one verse to keep. It goes well with another parent or a small group of parents; each session has a guide for a group at the bottom.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a group of parents through For parents: leading faith at home, or two parents working through it together. The group is for parents and grandparents of children of any age, whether they grew up in church or never saw faith at home at all. A leader doesn't need to be a model parent. A leader needs to be honest about their own failures, gentle with others' guilt, and steady in pointing past technique to the grace of God.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what happened at home that week, using the group guide for each session, gathered below in order.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten parents is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for eight meetings, and keep the end time you promised, since babysitters and bedtimes are waiting. If couples come together, let each speak for themselves. Make room for single parents and for parents whose spouse doesn't share their faith; they should never feel like the exception in the room.

sections.title: The room
body: A living room, a kitchen table or a quiet corner of a church works well. If you can arrange childcare in another room, parents will listen better. Say plainly at the first meeting that no one's family is on trial, that anyone may pass on any question, that what is said about children and marriages stays in the room unless someone is in danger, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: how last week's one thing to do went at home, the good nights and the ones that fell apart.
Five minutes: one person reads the session's verse aloud.
Thirty minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order, leaving room for what parents bring.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, praying for children by name. Nobody has to pray aloud.
Ten minutes: name the next session and its one thing to do, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Parents ask hard questions about their own children: why one child believes and another doesn't, whether they ruined something early on, what to say about death, divorce or a parent who left. Don't offer formulas. Proverbs describes how life tends to go; it does not guarantee how a child will turn out, and no parent should be told that a child's unbelief proves their failure.

Where Christians differ, as they do on methods of discipline, the baptism of children and when a child should share the Lord's Supper, say what they share and that faithful parents differ, and send each family to their own pastor. The track takes no side on these.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: A parents' group will meet real pain: a child who has walked away from faith, a marriage under strain, a child with a disability or an illness, a parent grieving a child, a home where anger has frightened someone. When that comes into the room, stop and listen. Don't explain it, don't fix it, and don't hurry back to the session. Ask whether the group should go on or pause, and speak with the person afterwards.

If anyone says that a child is being harmed, or that they or a child are not safe at home, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the police and child protection services, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point a parent to Find Help when what they carry has grown too heavy: a child who speaks of not wanting to live, anger at home that someone cannot control, harm done to a child, a marriage where someone is afraid, grief that has taken their sleep, or a parent who no longer wants to go on. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: Leading when no one showed you how
teaching: Many parents who want faith at home never saw it done. No one prayed at their table or opened a Bible after dinner, and the whole idea feels like a costume that doesn't fit. Yet leading faith at home was never meant for experts. When Martin Luther found in 1529 that ordinary people in the village parishes of Saxony knew almost nothing of the faith, he wrote the Small Catechism for the head of each household to teach at home. He assumed ordinary parents could do it, with a short book and a few minutes a day.

The awkwardness is normal, and it fades. Children don't need a polished leader; they need a parent who is plainly under the same word being read to them. Say so when you don't know an answer. Let a child read the verse or choose the song. Keep the same time and the same order, so that it becomes part of the furniture of the day. Joshua's resolve was a household's, not a scholar's: “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Leading begins with deciding, and the rest is learned by doing it badly for a while.

sessions.do: Choose one meal or one bedtime this week. Read a few verses aloud, ask one question, and pray one sentence. Do it three times before you judge how it went.

sessions.title: Faith at each age
teaching: Children take in the faith differently at different ages, and a parent who knows that can stop expecting a four-year-old to sit like a teenager. From about three to six, children learn through story, song, repetition and touch. They can learn that God made them, loves them and is near, and they can learn a short answer by heart long before they understand it. From seven to eleven, children want to know how things work and whether they're true. They can read a passage, follow the Bible's story from beginning to end, and ask why, and they deserve real answers.

From twelve to sixteen, young people begin to think about thinking. They notice contradictions, test what they were told, and want to be asked what they think, not only told. Talk less, ask more, and let silence sit. The site has something for each stage. For the youngest, tonight's devotion and the catechism's shorter answers. For seven to sixteen, the Bible Explorer, which tells the Bible as one story on a map. And the family reading plans take a household through Mark, the Psalms and the Old Testament story.

sessions.title: A child's hard question
teaching: Children ask the questions adults have learned to stop asking. Who made God? Why can't we see him? What happens when we die? Does God still love a child who does wrong? Why doesn't he answer? A parent's instinct is often to close the question quickly, with a pat answer or a change of subject, because the question unsettles the parent more than the child. Scripture expects the questions. Moses told Israel what to do “when your son asks” (Deuteronomy 6:20): tell him the story of how the LORD brought his people out of Egypt.

An honest answer has three parts. Say what Christians believe, in words the child can hold. Say plainly what no one fully knows, because a child who catches you bluffing will stop asking. And say what you trust about God even where you can't see the whole answer. Then ask what made them wonder. Often the question underneath is about a grandparent who is ill or something a friend said at school. The Bible Explorer has short films made for exactly these questions, for watching together and talking over afterwards.

sessions.do: Watch one of the question films with your child this week, then ask what they thought, and listen before you add anything.

sessions.title: When a teenager doubts
teaching: A teenager who doubts is often doing what a teenager should do: testing whether the faith they were handed is their own. Many parents hear the first hard question as a door slamming, and react with alarm, pressure or a lecture, which can turn a question into a wall. The church has a long memory of doubt held inside faith. The psalmists argue with God, Thomas asked to see the wounds, and Jude tells the church, “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 1:22). Mercy here isn't softness about truth. It's patience with a person.

Stay close more than you argue. Keep eating together, keep driving them places, keep asking what they think and listening to the end. Take their objection seriously enough to look into it with them; the case for the faith on this site was written for honest questions. Don't make your love depend on where they land, and don't hide your own faith either. Let them see you pray and read and keep going to church because you believe it, not to manage them. Their faith, if it comes, has to be theirs. Yours is the steady home it can come back to.

verse.text: And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Your own faith is what they watch
teaching: Children learn more from what their parents love than from what their parents say. They notice whether a parent prays when no one is watching, whether Sunday gives way to every other plan, how a parent speaks about people who aren't in the room, and what happens after a parent loses their temper. Paul could tell the Corinthians, “You are to imitate me, just as I imitate Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1), and every parent says something like that whether they mean to or not. The question isn't whether children are watching. It's what they're seeing.

This isn't a call to perform. A child can tell a parent who is acting from one who is living, and performance teaches only that faith is a show. The most formative thing a parent can do is keep their own life with God honest and visible: reading Scripture where the children can see it, praying about real things, owning it when they've wronged someone, apologizing to the children themselves. A tired parent who keeps returning to God teaches more than an impressive one who never seems to need him. Begin with your own soul, and the home will feel it.

sessions.title: Discipline and grace
teaching: Discipline is part of love, and Scripture never pretends otherwise: “No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). But discipline can aim at the wrong target. A parent can train a child to behave in front of others while leaving the heart untouched, or rule by anger until the child learns only to hide. Paul warns, “Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged” (Colossians 3:21). The aim is a heart, not a performance.

Grace changes how discipline feels from the inside. A child corrected by a parent who is calm, clear and quick to restore learns that wrongdoing is serious and that love isn't withdrawn. Name the wrong, give a fitting consequence, and then close it, with no grudge carried to breakfast. When the parent is the one who got it wrong, apologize to the child plainly. Christian parents differ on methods, including whether to spank, and faithful parents hold both views. Whatever the method, no child should be afraid of a parent's anger.

sessions.question: When you correct your children, what are you usually aiming at: their behavior, your own peace, or their heart?
sessions.do: The next time you correct a child, finish by restoring them on purpose: say the matter is closed and show it. If you owe a child an apology, give it this week.

care: If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Parenting alone, or as the only believer
teaching: Many parents lead faith at home alone. Some are single through death, divorce or a choice that wasn't theirs. Some are married to a spouse who doesn't believe, or who believes but won't lead. If that's you, hear it plainly: you are not running a lesser version of a Christian home. Paul traces Timothy's faith to the women of his house: “your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Acts says only that his father was a Greek. God has always worked through whoever is there.

If your spouse doesn't share your faith, honor them in front of the children. Don't make the children choose, and don't turn devotions into a quiet campaign against the other parent. Paul told believers married to unbelievers that their children are holy (1 Corinthians 7:14), a word of hope rather than a formula. If you're parenting alone, you'll be tired in ways two-parent homes rarely see, so keep it small and ask for help. A church family can supply what one parent can't: another adult who prays for your child by name, a mentor, a seat at someone's table.

sessions.title: Handing it on
teaching: Faith has always been handed on at home. Deuteronomy tells parents to teach God's words to their children at home and on the road, and Psalm 78 promises not to hide God's works from the next generation, so “that the coming generation would know them” (Psalm 78:6). Then the psalm does something surprising. It tells the story of Israel's failures, generation after generation, so that the children would not be stubborn as their fathers were. Handing on the faith includes handing on the honest record: the ways a family and a church have gone wrong, and been met by mercy.

You will not finish this work, and you aren't meant to. A child's faith is finally God's gift, not a parent's achievement. Some children wander a long way before they come home, and some seem never to, and that isn't the measure of whether you were faithful. Your part is to keep telling the story, keep praying, keep the table set, and leave the rest with the God who has kept his promises to every generation before yours. The faith confessed in the Apostles' Creed reached you through people you will never meet. Hand it on.
